analysis.one_liner: Bans Members of Congress and their families from trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: Fourteen cosponsors from both parties backed a ban on congressional stock trading, but a year after its introduction the bill sits in two House committees with no hearing and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar Members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependents from buying or selling individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, or similar investments. They would have 90 days to sell what they hold or move it into an approved blind trust, though they could still own diversified mutual funds, Treasury bonds, municipal bonds, and their federal retirement plan. An ethics office would post compliance certificates online, and willful violators could face civil penalties of up to $50,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, in the form of a Congress whose lawmakers cannot personally profit from the industries and companies their votes affect. Members' financial conflicts of interest — real or perceived — would be removed, and compliance certificates would be posted publicly so voters could check. Honest Members also gain a clear rule that shields them from suspicion.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting a Congress free of stock conflicts

how_it_helps.text: It bans Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependents from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, and synthetic look-alike investments, closing the current system in which lawmakers may trade while their votes move those companies' prices.

Members would have 90 days to divest by selling or placing assets in an ethics-approved blind trust, and trustees could not tell Members what their trust holds — cutting off the information channel that makes 'blind' trusts leaky.

The ethics office must publish compliance certificates on a public website, and willful violators can be referred to the Attorney General for a civil action with penalties up to $50,000 that cannot be paid from official or campaign funds.
Losses from any violating stock transaction could not be deducted from income taxes, removing a way to write off forbidden trades.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their families, who would have to sell individual holdings or lock them into blind trusts within 90 days, and could owe civil penalties up to $50,000 for willful violations. The bill softens this with a tax-deferral provision that lets divesting Members postpone capital gains taxes on forced sales — a cost largely borne by Members' own portfolios rather than by any industry or the public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The $50,000 penalty cap is small compared with many Members' portfolios, and enforcement runs through the Attorney General, a politically appointed official who may choose not to sue colleagues' violations.

Members who divest get a tax deferral on capital gains from forced sales under an expanded conflict-of-interest tax rule — a benefit available only to the relatively wealthy people who must divest in the first place.
The bill covers only Members, spouses, and dependents — not congressional staff, and not executive branch officials — so officials who shape policy day to day could still hold the same conflicts.

Members could still park unlimited money in broadly diversified funds that own the very companies they regulate, so economic exposure to market outcomes does not disappear; it just becomes blind and indirect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing lawmakers' personal financial stake in the companies their votes affect — is broad and meaningful for public trust, even though it is hard to measure in dollars. The costs fall almost entirely on Members' own portfolios, and the bill deliberately eases even those: forced divestitures get tax deferral, diversified funds stay permitted, and penalties are capped. Its honest weaknesses are enforcement (an Attorney General decides whether to sue) and scope (no staff or executive officials). On balance a well-designed, if not airtight, integrity measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees in January 2025, and neither committee has held a hearing or a vote on it since.

narrative.text: On January 9, 2025, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) introduced the bill with Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), Cory Mills (R-LA), and Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL) as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Ways and Means; the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor vote afterward.
Fourteen members had signed on as cosponsors by the record date, 11 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but no committee or floor action followed.
Past Congresses have seen similar congressional stock-trading bans draw broad bipartisan support and still never reach a floor vote, and this bill now sits in the same position.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress are better off so far: they keep the current rules, under which they and their families can freely trade individual stocks. House leaders and the two committee chairs who never scheduled action also avoided a vote on a proposal many colleagues might have found uncomfortable.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress keep their trading freedom

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors from both parties.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the ban.

against.what_they_did: Has not brought any congressional stock-trading ban to the House floor despite multiple bipartisan versions pending this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan split on the bill itself is unknown; its sponsorship was bipartisan, with 11 of 14 cosponsors Democrats and 3 Republicans.

industries.industry: Sitting Members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The bill's rules apply to the people who write them: Members and their families would have to give up individual stock trading, divest within 90 days, publish proof of compliance, and risk $50,000 civil penalties. Their financial interest runs directly against the bill's purpose.

industries.industry: Mutual fund and diversified investment fund industry
industries.note: Diversified registered funds are written into the bill as the exception to the ban, so money that would otherwise sit in individual stocks gets steered toward fund companies, Treasuries, and the federal Thrift Savings Plan. This gain does not come at the public's expense.

Roughly 535 House and Senate households would stop trading individual securities, costing brokerages some commissions and margin business. The dollar impact is small, which is why brokerages rather than Members are not the main obstacle to the bill.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a long odds path unless House leadership changes course. It must clear two committees — Ways and Means because of its tax provision — and similar bipartisan stock-trading bans in recent Congresses have repeatedly died in committee despite dozens of cosponsors. It could become part of a larger package if leadership chooses to attach it to something that must pass, but a standalone vote is unlikely under current scheduling.
